questions.q: What does an HTTP status code in the 4xx range generally indicate?
options: The request succeeded
A problem with the client's request itself (bad input, missing authentication, wrong URL, etc.)
A problem on the server's side, unrelated to what the client sent
The request is still in progress
questions.explain: 4xx (client error) codes indicate the request itself was the problem — things like 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, or 404 Not Found — as opposed to 5xx, which indicates a server-side failure.

It prints the status code without taking any other action
It raises an HTTPError if the status code is 4xx or 5xx, and does nothing if it's 2xx
It retries the request automatically up to three times
questions.explain: raise_for_status() checks the response's status code and raises requests.exceptions.HTTPError only for error ranges (4xx/5xx); a successful 2xx response passes through with no exception.

questions.q: Which `requests` exception is the shared base class that every other `requests` exception (Timeout, ConnectionError, HTTPError) inherits from?
options: requests.exceptions.BaseError
requests.exceptions.RequestException
requests.exceptions.GenericError
Exception
questions.explain: requests.exceptions.RequestException is the base class for the library's exception hierarchy — catching it catches every more specific requests exception too, per the inheritance rule from Lesson 14.

questions.q: In an except chain with `except requests.exceptions.Timeout`, `except requests.exceptions.HTTPError`, and `except requests.exceptions.RequestException`, why must `RequestException` come LAST?
options: Python requires exceptions to be listed alphabetically
Because it's the broadest (base) class — if it came first, it would catch everything before the more specific except blocks ever got a chance to run
It doesn't matter; order has no effect on which except block runs
RequestException can only be used as the very first except clause
questions.explain: Python checks except clauses top to bottom and runs the first match. Since RequestException is the parent of Timeout and HTTPError, placing it first would catch those errors too, so the more specific handlers would never execute.

questions.q: What specifically does `requests.exceptions.Timeout` indicate, as opposed to `requests.exceptions.ConnectionError`?
options: Timeout means the request took longer than the specified timeout value; ConnectionError means the connection to the server couldn't be established at all
They are two names for the exact same situation
Timeout only happens on POST requests
ConnectionError means the JSON body was malformed
questions.explain: Timeout is raised when a request exceeds the time limit you set with timeout=. ConnectionError is a distinct failure — the connection to the server could not be made at all (network issue, DNS failure, bad host, etc.).
